doc.title: David Weiss interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 3, 2022

title: Rhythm sections and bassists: Dwayne Burno and drummers' tastes
summary: Asked who drives the rhythm, Weiss praises bassist Dwayne Burno, who improved his arrangements, and notes older drummers wanted a steady foundation.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: I love what you’re saying about this. And it makes me think about rhythm sections and what they do with the time. And I’m wondering, in your opinion, in the Cookers, who’s the main, who’s in the driver’s seat as far as the rhythm or is it a shared responsibility? And the reason I ask this is Cecil McBee said some very eloquent things about quarter notes, about playing the bass and approaching the quarter notes. And he said to the bassists, you are the timekeeper. You are the vibe of the entire group.

That’s true. I agree with that. I mean you know ask James Brown. I mean that comes, that’s a fact in a lot of music. The drummer seemingly is the guy, because he’s a little more easy to focus on him, plus with the fills and everything there’s more going on with the drummer. But the drummer can’t do that without the foundation from a bass player. And I have found, interestingly, and this is not, I mean you mentioned Cecil but this has got nothing to do with Cecil. What I have found over the years talking to various drummers is their taste in bass players is different than mine, or most people. Guys I think like Dwayne Burno is my guy. Like he’s a little younger than me but I’m going to say my generation. He was in all the bands I did and their inception, my octet and my sextet, he was the guy. He was the guy who took the Ron Carter stuff and made it a language and did the stuff that Ron did, which is rare, guys who are to do substitutions and do all that stuff. I mean I could play records and I did this with many big band albums, Wayne Shorter material, and I could point to parts in the arrangement where Dwayne made it better on the fly. Because he knew where everything was coming from and he understood what you were trying to do and he knew how to take it somewhere. And I could point to it and like I owe him ten dollars for that, because I didn’t write that, like in a soli section or something with the horns. He — it was like okay. I’ve even called him sometimes and I’d come to him and like, “Okay Dwayne, here you go. You own a piece of that.” But that said, I was shocked when drummers, you know, drummers generations before me who came out of that music that influenced Dwayne, they didn’t like playing with Dwayne. And he did, but some didn’t, like no, no, get this guy. And that

guy was just [hand motion straight ahead] you know because they wanted that to play off that. If Dwayne is busy doing, you know, what are they doing. One of them even said that like, “What am I gonna do?” You know?
They want to play with the time as opposed —
